observations.statement: States the overall estimand as the causal effect of the film's screenings on racial violence and Klan support, using an event-study design for short-run contemporaneous effects and a cross-sectional instrumental-variables design for longer-run Klan and hate outcomes.

Explains that a difference-in-differences design cannot be used for the long-run Klan outcome because no pre-period data exist before the organization's founding, and states this as the motivation for switching to a cross-sectional instrumental-variables strategy.

States that the event-study identification relies on a parallel-trends assumption together with county and state-by-week fixed effects, and explicitly notes that this design does not require the timing or location of the film's arrival to be uncorrelated with underlying local racism levels.

States that the theater-presence instrument must be both relevant and exogenous to unobserved determinants of Klan formation, and explicitly discusses the threat that theaters could have an independent effect on klavern formation through screenings of other influential films.

Frames the reduced-form comparisons between lynchings/riots and the IV klavern-formation estimates as mutually corroborating designs using a shared instrument, rather than as a single unified specification.
observations.locator: Section IV.C, Correspondence to Event Study Estimates

observations.statement: Cites external econometric guidance to support interpreting the two-stage least squares estimate as a local average treatment effect appropriate for a binary-outcome, binary-instrument setting.

Describes construction of the treatment-timing variable from newspaper advertisements gathered across three digitized newspaper archives plus a trade magazine, with research assistants visually inspecting search hits to confirm genuine screening advertisements.

States the event-study sample as a multi-year weekly county panel bracketing the film's road show, restricted to the continental United States, and notes in a footnote that including state fixed effects effectively removes one jurisdiction from identifying variation.
Restricts short-run treatment timing to a county's first showing of the film, explaining that the timing and location of return showings are less likely to be exogenous to local conditions.

Constructs the historical theater-stock instrument by merging a geocoded trade-magazine-based compilation of movie theaters with a separate crowd-sourced historical theater database used to fill gaps and extend coverage past the original source's cutoff year.

Notes that the klavern data record only the date a chapter was first mentioned, not its founding or dissolution date, and explicitly defines the primary long-run outcome as an indicator for whether a klavern had ever existed in a county by a fixed cutoff year given this limitation.

Defines the short-run outcomes as binary indicators for whether a lynching or race riot occurred in a county-week, choosing indicators rather than counts given the rarity of the underlying events, with count-based measures relegated to an appendix robustness check.
Defines the event-study treatment-timing variable using five-week bins centered on the week of the film's arrival rather than calendar months, with the exact binning rule spelled out in a footnote.

Defines the primary instrument as a binary indicator for whether a county had any theater the year before the film's release, and separately constructs intensive-margin alternative instruments (theaters per capita, maximum seating capacity, opening year) for robustness.

Builds a state-level Klan-intensity outcome by normalizing chapter or membership figures against an eligible-population denominator of US-born White men, an implicit standardization intended to make cross-area comparisons meaningful.

Constructs long-run hate-crime outcomes as annual counts scaled to a per-population rate and disaggregates them by the victim group's racial or religious category to separate anti-Black incidents from other targeted violence.

Reports the event-study fixed effects (county and state-by-week) directly alongside the estimating equation in the main text, with the clustering choice stated in the same passage rather than left only to a table footnote.

Presents a summary-statistics table comparing treatment and control counties, with a separate comparison restricted to control counties that had a theater, aiming to isolate selection on theater presence from selection on screening status itself.

Progresses the first-stage table across columns by sequentially adding demographic, social-capital, media, and racism control blocks, reporting the dependent-variable mean and adjusted R-squared in every column alongside the coefficient of interest.

Presents the main klavern-formation table in three stacked panels (OLS, reduced form, 2SLS) sharing the same sample restrictions across columns, with each column's sample restriction named directly in a row label and the dependent-variable mean and first-stage statistic reported for every specification.
States the clustering level and reports a weak-instrument diagnostic in the notes of every instrumental-variables table, rather than describing the inference approach only once in the main text.

Clusters standard errors by state throughout the paper without an extended discussion of why the state, rather than county or region, is the chosen clustering level, beyond noting the state fixed effects used in the design.

Supplements cluster-robust inference for the short-run design with a permutation-based randomization-inference procedure that reassigns placebo treatment dates drawn from the empirical distribution of actual treatment timing.

Reports robustness to potential spatial correlation as a distinct check rather than as the baseline inference choice, including a spatial-autocorrelation diagnostic, county-clustered errors, a bandwidth-based spatial adjustment, and a worst-case spatial-correlation confidence interval method.
Does not discuss a multiple-testing adjustment anywhere in the text despite reporting many outcome variables and many robustness specifications across the short-run and long-run designs.

Reports a graphical pre-trends check in the main event-study figure and describes a supplementary longer-horizon pre-trends check placed in the online appendix, both offered as support for the parallel-trends assumption.
Reports a weak-instrument F-statistic in every column of the first-stage table and states the benchmark literature used to judge whether the instrument is sufficiently strong.

Reports an exogeneity test comparing the reduced-form relationship between the instrument and the long-run outcome inside a state where the film was banned versus all other states, using the ban as a test of the exclusion restriction.

Reports a timing-based placebo diagnostic showing that only theaters opened before the end of the film's road show predict the long-run outcome, while theaters opened afterward do not, offered as further exogeneity evidence.

Reports an outcome-based placebo test using screenings of an unrelated contemporaneous popular film for the short-run violence design, and a separate placebo check for the long-run Klan design using the same film's screenings.

Reports a formal coefficient-stability statistic for selection on unobservables computed from the unmatched and propensity-score-matched samples, alongside balance tables and density plots for the matched samples that are placed in the online appendix.

Summarizes a set of alternative-sample robustness checks for the short-run design (dropping neighboring counties, restricting to screened counties only, restricting to counties with digitized newspaper coverage) that are placed entirely in the online appendix and only described narratively in the main text.

Summarizes alternative-specification checks for the short-run design (dropping state-by-week fixed effects, adding county-specific linear trends, allowing differential trends by historical discrimination) as a single appendix figure referenced narratively rather than reproduced in the main text.

Collects robustness of the long-run IV estimates to a set of alternative instruments (intensive-margin theater measures, opening-year measures, alternative-film-based instruments) in a single online appendix table.

Cross-validates the primary treatment-timing measure against an independently constructed screening dataset from a companion paper, reporting the two measures' agreement rate and re-running the main specification under the union, intersection, and each measure separately.

Discloses that the two independently constructed treatment datasets were developed by separate research teams working concurrently, who later coordinated to cross-check their measures against each other after independent development.

Reports propensity-score-matching estimates as an alternative-estimator robustness check for the long-run design, run across three different comparison-group definitions and both with and without additional covariate adjustment.

Reports heterogeneous instrumental-variables estimates for klavern formation split by above/below-median values of several demographic, geographic, and historical-racism covariates plus a former-Confederate-state indicator, presented as a single coefficient-plot figure.

Frames the religious-participation heterogeneity result as motivated by a social-capital mechanism hypothesis about the film's catalyzing effect, rather than as a subgroup analysis specified in advance.

Reports separate heterogeneity results for third-KKK persistence in later decades and notes that the pattern of subgroup effects differs from the second-KKK heterogeneity results, interpreting the difference as reflecting conditions for institutional persistence rather than initial catalyzation.

Presents evidence of media imitation as a mechanism using an intermediate outcome unrelated to violence or membership counts (a shift in census naming patterns), explicitly offered as corroborating rather than primary causal evidence.

States at the outset of the mechanisms section that data constraints prevent a comprehensive test of channels, and explicitly labels the discussion of coordination, imitation, and persuasion channels as suggestive rather than conclusive.

Uses survey-based attitude data from later decades as an indirect proxy for contemporaneous persuasion effects, explicitly noting that no contemporaneous survey of racial attitudes exists for the period under study.

Applies a formal causal-mediation-analysis framework from a cited methodological paper to decompose the long-run hate outcome into effects operating through historical klavern formation versus other channels, explicitly flagging the strong identifying assumptions the method requires.
Interprets short-run violence effects relative to the sample mean of each outcome rather than in raw levels, motivated by the rarity of the underlying events.

Interprets long-run klavern and hate-crime effects relative to both the sample mean and the raw treatment-control difference, explicitly comparing the instrumented estimate's magnitude to the unconditional gap between groups.

Converts a state-level instrumental-variables estimate into a persuasion-rate metric using an established framework from the media-persuasion literature, and explicitly benchmarks the resulting rate against the range reported in a survey of media-persuasion studies.

Provides a back-of-envelope aggregate estimate of the scale of people affected by scaling per-county point estimates by population figures, explicitly presented as an approximation rather than a precise count.

Acknowledges that no comprehensive historical dataset of milder forms of racial violence exists, explaining that the short-run analysis is therefore restricted to lynchings and riots even though the true effect on racial intimidation is likely broader.

States explicitly that mechanism evidence on persuasion is only suggestive because the available historical measures of racial attitudes are coarse and represent the views of a small, non-representative share of the population.

Discusses the historical specificity of the setting, an early-twentieth-century road-show distribution system with limited theater penetration, as a scope condition distinguishing this evidence from studies of modern, already media-saturated markets.
Uses event-study coefficient plots with confidence intervals as the primary presentation format for the short-run design rather than a single-coefficient regression table.
Uses paired choropleth maps to visualize the geographic footprint of both the film's road show and the second Klan's chapter locations, presented together early in the data section.

Reports standard errors in parentheses beneath every coefficient directly in the regression tables, with notes in each table stating the clustering level and the composition of control blocks rather than relegating that information to a separate methods appendix.

Previews the paper's main qualitative findings (short-run violence spike, long-run Klan formation, and persistence into modern hate crimes) in the introduction before presenting any results in the body of the paper.

Places a stand-alone contribution paragraph enumerating three separate literatures the paper claims to contribute to, followed by a roadmap paragraph outlining section order, at the end of the introduction.

Treats robustness checks for each empirical design as their own labeled subsection following the corresponding main-results subsection, rather than interleaving robustness discussion with the main results.

Relies heavily on the online appendix for supporting figures and tables referenced repeatedly throughout the main text, which is explicitly flagged at the end of the introduction as containing additional material not part of the reviewed text.
Cites a formal archived replication-data deposit for the paper in the reference list rather than including a dedicated data-and-code availability statement in the body of the article.

Draws underlying data from a mix of publicly available digitized newspaper archives, publicly compiled historical registers, and public administrative crime-reporting data, without describing any restricted-access or application-based data source.

gaps: No statistical software (e.g., Stata, R) is named anywhere in the main text, even though the paper is a code-based empirical study with a cited replication package.

No dedicated data-and-code availability statement appears in the article body describing what the replication package contains or how to obtain it; only a bibliographic citation of the archived replication data appears in the reference list.

No pre-analysis plan, IRB approval, or participant-consent statement appears anywhere in the text; the study uses archival and administrative historical data rather than a researcher-run experiment or survey.
No explicit justification for choosing the state as the standard-error clustering level appears in the main text beyond its role as a fixed-effects dimension in the design.

No explicit multiple-testing adjustment is discussed despite many outcome variables (lynchings, riots, homicides, klaverns, disaggregated hate crimes) and many robustness specifications being reported across the paper.

The extracted text contains only the published article; the online Appendix referenced dozens of times (additional figures, tables, and robustness checks) is not part of this text and was not read, so appendix-only claims are recorded as basis stated with tags in_appendix and online_appendix_not_available.

reading.note: All 37 pages of the extracted published article were read in full: title, abstract, introduction, Section I background, Section II data, Sections III and IV empirical strategy/results/robustness for short-run and long-run designs, Section V mechanisms, Section VI long-run effects and persistence, Section VII conclusion, and the reference list. The online Appendix cited throughout (additional figures A.I-A.XXV and tables A.I-A.XVII) is not included in this text file and was not read; coverage is therefore main_text rather than full.
